newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Hashimoto under pressure on budget.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Hashimoto under pressure on budget.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, returning on Tuesday from a Southeast Asian tour, faced pressure to rethink his budget, implement real reforms and ease fears about the economy now battering the Tokyo stock market.
Analysts said, however, that the opposition camp looked in too much disarray to profit much from the mistrust of policy behind the share price slump when parliament opens next week.

And while Hashimoto could face calls from members of his own Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) to alter the budget should share prices slide towards a financial danger zone, making more than modest changes would carry political risks, some added.

"If the Nikkei falls below 16,000, we will hear many conservative politicians again demanding a freeze on the consumption tax and/or maintenance of the temporary income tax cut for another year," wrote SBC Warburg Japan political analyst Shigenori Okazaki. "However, this would entail a huge political risk for Hashimoto."

The Tokyo market's main barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, lost more than 2,000 points last week on persistent doubts over both the government's ability to craft a quick market fix and its commitment to more deep-rooted reforms.
On Monday, the Nikkei rebounded more than 800 points, but closed marginally lower on Tuesday on renewed worries.

Much of the recent market pessimism was sparked by the government's proposed tight budget for 1997/98, which aims at getting the nation's big budget deficit under control. The Finance Ministry's draft budget was approved by the cabinet last month and should be passed by parliament before March 31.

Concern has focused not only on fears that a rise in the sales tax on April 1 and an end to special income tax cuts could stall the recovery in its tracks, but also on a lack of commitment to reform. This was signalled by failure to reject pleas to fund special interests' pet projects.

A survey by daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun released on Tuesday showed voter support for Hashimoto at a robust 47.1 percent. But 86 percent said his economic policies were insufficient and 71.3 percent urged changes in the budget.
Of those seeking budget revisions, 43.4 percent said the rise in the sales tax to five percent from three percent should be put off and the income tax cuts kept in place, it said.
Quicker movement on deregulation was urged by 21.5 percent, while 5.8 percent wanted a stock market bailout and only 3.4 percent urged more public works spending to boost the economy.

Public dislike of the budget appears ready-made ammunition for the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), which urged freezing the sales tax and enacting 18 trillion yen ($155 billion) in tax cuts in its October election campaign.

That supply-side platform, however, did little to attract votes and the party won only 156 seats in parliament's 500-seat Lower House against 239 for the LDP. Since then, Shinshinto has been plagued by infighting and defections, seeing its Lower House seats dwindle to 142 in the last month.
The fledgling Democratic Party, a reformist group with 52 seats in the Lower House, may also have trouble attacking the sales tax, which it supported during the October election.
Hashimoto and his ministers have sought to ease market anxiety with assurances over the economy and pledges of structural reform and financial deregulation.

But LDP politicians are showing signs of jitters. On Tuesday, the party's policy chief urged the government to seek ways to tackle weak stock prices. Hashimoto was expected to meet Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and his chief cabinet secretary after returning on Tuesday night from an Asian tour.

Economists said a further share slump might push the government to reverse its decision to end two trillion yen ($17.2 billion) in special income tax cuts. But they said there was little chance the sales tax rise would be put off, and that anyway what was really needed was swift action on deregulation.
Analysts say 15,000 or so on the Nikkei is a critical level where banks' hidden profits on shares vanish, crippling their ability to write off bad loans and putting many in the red.

"Basically there is no chance of the consumption tax rise being postponed," said Peter Morgan, an economist at brokerage James Capel Pacific. "There ought to be at least some chance of the income tax cuts being continued, but it's got to be significantly less than 50 percent at this point." ($1=116 yen)
